content: Several companies are currently manufacturing and selling electronic cigarettes, which are devices designed to mimic the experience of smoking traditional cigarettes. These devices are shaped like small rods, slightly longer than a conventional cigarette. The mouthpiece of the e-cigarette contains a replaceable cartridge filled with a liquid solution. This liquid typically consists of nicotine and propylene glycol as its primary components. When a user inhales through the device, the airflow is detected by an internal microprocessor. This microprocessor activates an atomizer, which disperses tiny droplets of the liquid into the air stream, creating a vapor mist. The user then inhales this vapor. The inclusion of propylene glycol in the liquid formulation enhances the visual resemblance of the vapor to traditional cigarette smoke. Additionally, the microprocessor activates an orange LED at the tip of the device, simulating the glowing ember of a lit cigarette. The vapor produced not only visually mimics cigarette smoke but also approximates the temperature of smoke from a conventional cigarette, typically between 50-60°C. The device is powered by a rechargeable battery, and the underlying technology is protected under European Patent EP 1 618 803 A1. The nicotine solution cartridges used in e-cigarettes are formulated based on specific recipes, as outlined in the patent. These cartridges are designed to deliver nicotine to the user in a controlled manner. E-cigarettes are often marketed as a healthier alternative to traditional tobacco smoking. This claim is based on the fact that the atomization process used in e-cigarettes does not produce the particulate matter associated with the combustion of plant material, which occurs in conventional smoking. A toxicity study on the nicotine solutions used in e-cigarettes has been conducted by Professor Dr. Bernd Mayer, though the details of this study are not provided here. In the European Union, the legal status of e-cigarettes has been subject to regulatory scrutiny. According to the EC Directive 93/42/EEC, e-cigarettes are classified as Class IIa medical devices, as they are intended to administer medicinal substances (in this case, nicotine) to the human body. Furthermore, the nicotine cartridges are considered medicinal products under EC Directive 2001/83/EG, as the nicotine is delivered in a solution form rather than derived directly from tobacco plants. Based on these classifications, e-cigarettes must obtain CE marking before they can be distributed, and the nicotine cartridges require registration as medicinal products. The Austrian Agency for Healthcare Safety issued a decision on April 18, 2007, affirming this regulatory interpretation. Since this decision was made by a competent authority in one EU country, it serves as a guideline for other EU member states. However, as of now, no e-cigarette products have obtained the necessary medical device certification or medicinal product registration. Consequently, the distribution of e-cigarettes within the European Union is currently considered illegal. Several companies are involved in the production and distribution of e-cigarettes. These include: Cigartex (France) Crown Seven (USA) EMTAC (Germany) Rooney (Belgium) Rutoo E-cigarette (Europe) Smuke Europe Ltd (Portugal) Fujian Mondex Ltd (China, Wholesale) Sedansa (Belgium) Sottera Njoy (USA) SuperSmoker (Belgium) e-Cig org (USA)
